title: Why Do Ships Have a Bulb Under the Front?
description:
When a giant ship sits in dry dock, you can see something strange below the waterline. At the very front, a huge rounded bulb sticks out, like the nose of a dolphin. You never see it when the ship is sailing. But it saves enormous amounts of fuel on every trip. Today, ten parts of a ship, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 10 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
0:57 1. The bulbous bow
2:06 2. The giant propeller
3:16 3. The bow thruster
4:22 4. The load line
5:30 5. The rudder
6:38 6. The propeller nozzle
7:42 7. The anchor chain
8:45 8. The sacrificial anodes
9:46 9. The bridge wings
10:47 10. The double hull
11:59 The verdict

Sources:
- Bulbous bow, wave cancellation, slow steaming retrofits: Wikipedia, "Bulbous bow" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulbous_bow
- Ship propellers and cavitation: Wikipedia, "Propeller" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propeller and "Cavitation" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavitation
- Bow thrusters: Wikipedia, "Bow thruster" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_thruster
- Load line and Samuel Plimsoll: Wikipedia, "Waterline" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterline#Load_lines and "Samuel Plimsoll" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Plimsoll
- Rudders: Wikipedia, "Rudder" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudder
- Kort nozzle (Ludwig Kort): Wikipedia, "Kort nozzle" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kort_nozzle
- Anchor chain and scope: Wikipedia, "Anchor" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchor
- Sacrificial anodes: Wikipedia, "Galvanic anode" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galvanic_anode
- Bridge wings and SOLAS visibility: Wikipedia, "Bridge (nautical)" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_(nautical)
- Double hulls, Exxon Valdez, Oil Pollution Act 1990, MARPOL: Wikipedia, "Double hull" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_hull
